A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MAUBERT research and contain complete, readable main text and Appendices A–F. Text extraction and rendered-page comparison support matching all figures, tables, and mathematical content.

before.justification: v2 reports original recognition and ABX experiments, phonetic inventory discovery, and spoken language modelling and DiscoPhon results, including Tables 7–13 in the appendices.

after.justification: v3 retains these original empirical evaluations and reports revised phone-accuracy values in Table 1.

M1.justification: The documented adaptation procedure changes the student feature extractor from frozen in v2 Figure 1b to trainable in v3, consistent with revised Section 5.1. The architecture, losses, and pseudo-label methods remain unchanged. The PDFs do not establish whether this reflects retraining or correction of the earlier description.

E1.justification: Training languages and evaluation coverage are unchanged: multilingual recognition, development and ZRC 2017 ABX tasks, English/French read and casual speech, and the appendix inventory, spoken language modelling, and DiscoPhon evaluations.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged in the corresponding experiments. Table 3 retains MFCC, HuBERT-base, MMS-1B, XEUS, and mHuBERT-147; the speech-register, spoken language modelling, and DiscoPhon comparison tables also retain their comparator rows.

E3.justification: Section 5.1 revises the reported self-supervised fine-tuning configuration from training the Transformer encoder to training HuBERT modules including the feature extractor. This changes an explicitly documented freezing setting without establishing that experiments were rerun. Training budgets, optimizers, splits, and evaluation metrics are otherwise unchanged.

E4.justification: The BLSTM ablation account, speaker/context analyses, speech-register comparisons, and inventory threshold analyses and examples are retained. No new ablation, robustness test, or case study appears in the appendices.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or formal significance tests. Reporting of averages across languages and speaker conditions is unchanged.

E6.justification: Table 1 substantially revises the comparison between model variants: FEAT phone accuracy changes from 72.28% to 82.35% on held-out training-language data and from 51.20% to 66.74% on development languages. With PHONE scores unchanged, its advantages shrink from 10.44 and 15.95 percentage points to 0.37 and 0.41, changing a large deficit into near parity. Other experimental results, including the appendix tables, are unchanged; these revised scores do not establish a newly achieved performance gain.

T1.justification: The mathematical descriptions, including language sampling in Appendix B and feature-vector thresholding and distances in Appendix C, are unchanged. No formal assumption, derivation, theorem, or proof is added or revised.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution statements, and conclusion retain the same claims about multilingual phonetic representations, contextual invariance, and effective adaptation with limited unlabelled speech.

C2.justification: Section 4.3 replaces the interpretation that PHONE's accuracy advantage grows on development languages with a small, stable advantage across language sets. It also adds accumulated frame-level errors as an explanation for the larger PER gap. Broader discussion, limitations, and appendix interpretations are unchanged.

D1.justification: New footnote 6 explicitly states that the feature extractor is updated during fine-tuning, unlike pre-training, and Section 5.1 identifies the trained HuBERT modules. This improves implementation specificity; hardware, hyperparameter tables, preprocessing instructions, and code-access information remain unchanged.

R1.justification: The cited works and substantive positioning relative to multilingual SSL, articulatory-feature learning, and speech-representation evaluation are unchanged. No references are added or removed.

P1.justification: Local edits revise Sections 4.3 and 5.1, replace percentage notation with percentage points for differences, and correct an Appendix A cross-reference to Table 5. The introduction's cited phoneme-count range changes from 30–80 to 10–100. Section organization and the overall narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: Figure 1b changes the student feature extractor's frozen marker to a trainable marker, and its caption replaces 'Transformer' with 'encoder'. The added footnote produces small text-flow changes. Other figures and table designs are unchanged.

improvement.justification: v3 improves reporting through explicit fine-tuning trainability, clearer percentage-point comparisons, and interpretation aligned with the revised Table 1 values. These changes help readers understand and reproduce the work while retaining its benchmark and appendix evidence. The PDFs do not explain whether the revised values and training description reflect reruns, so higher reported accuracy alone does not establish improved scientific quality.
